Presidential Ramblings
By Steve Hansen
Greetings and Happy New Year,
Next month we have our AGM and with it an opportunity for new people to jump on board to help
steer and run our organisation. I am delighted to
say we have secured a nomination for President
and we have other openings for Secretary and
Members at Large. We have other roles in the Guild
that do not necessarily needing filled by Board
members. For instance, we continue to seek a
greeter for our in person Guild Nights. The role is
easy and everyone is qualified. All you have to do is
regularly attend Guild Nights - that’s nine meetings
per year - and say hello to new faces as they walk
in. Sourcing and collecting wood for our classes is
another important task that arises now and then.
There are many other smaller roles that are currently being done by a handful of people that already have quite a lot on their plate. You probably
know who they are, so why not ask them how you
can help.
The President’s Challenge for February is “musical”.
Steve

Editor’s Notes
By Steve Fairbairn
Happy New Year! I hope you all had a restful holiday season and are well on the way to breaking all
of your New Year resolutions.
We have some really great articles this month
along with a larger than usual gallery.
I’ve been editing and publishing the GVWG newsletter for a little over 5 years. I feel like it is time
for a new editor/publisher to take over and put
their personal stamp on it before the end of 2026.
If you are interested, or even curious as to what
the role entails, please contact me at editor@gvwg.ca or approach me at a monthly
meeting.
Steve

Organic Fantasy
By Steve Hansen
Our Guild had its first meeting in September of
1999. Soon thereafter, we started planning an entry for the AAW Collaborative Challenge for the upcoming Summer Symposium. The project chosen
was a hand-crank pipe organ which we codenamed “The Fast Ferry Project”. Headed by Bruce
Campbell along with several team leads, twenty
eight members took part in its design and manufacture. The completed organ was presented by Art
Liestman at the AAW Symposium in Charlotte,
North Carolina, the summer of 2000 as Organic
Fantasy. Awarded an Honorary Mention, it was
sold via the AAW Education Fund auction to Jayne
Hart of Virginia, an enthusiastic organist and it
adorned her home for 23 years. Because of moving
and downsizing Jayne reached out to us in 2023 to
see if we would like it back. We heartily accepted
her generous offer and undertook the task of figuring out how to get it back to Vancouver. Serendipity would strike three times to make this feasible.
First, Jayne still had the original shipping crate, custom built by us in 2000! Second, Art connected us
with Denis Delehanty-AAW member and past AAW
Board member-and he kindly stepped in and
offered herculean assistance in collecting the organ
and re-packing it for shipment. And finally, Denis’s
wife through her knowledge of freight forwarding
was able to secure a highly discounted fee to have
it shipped! Thank you to the Delehantys!
Organic Fantasy landed back in Canada in February,
2024. After 25 years the instrument is in need of
restoration. The hope is that it can be put back in
presentable order and most importantly find a new
home for this important piece of Guild history.
Again, we are indebted to Denis Delehanty for his
help in securing and returning our very first Collaborative Challenge project!
Here is the build team from 2000:
Dave Armitage, Fred Baldwin, Marco Berera, John
Bese, Brian Billington, Don Bishop, Bruce Campbell,
Neno Catania, Les Crossley, Mike (Ace) Dawson,
Colin Delory, Sandy Dougal, John Flanagan, Klaas
Focker, Andrew Forrest, Andrew Forsyth, Ted
Fromson, Steve Hansen, Don Hoskins, Phil Laliberte, David MacDonald, Ross Pilgrim, Rich Schmid,
Bob Vergette, Art Liestman, Ludger Paus, Robert
Prinse, Larry Stevenson

January 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
1. Introduction: The Safety Journey
We all start with the basics: a sturdy face shield,
ideally a latheside dust collector and a ceiling dust
filtration, and the familiar N95 or N100 mask when
sanding. These help with chips and reduce airborne
dust, but they have limits.
A face shield stops debris, but not the fine dust
from sanding and turning. Microscopic particles
under 2.5 microns linger in the air and can travel
deep into the lungs, where they are hardest to
clear. Dust collectors and ceiling filtration reduce
load, but can’t capture everything once dust escapes. Masks help, but they're hot, restrictive, and
fog my glasses.
I’m moving from occasional to regular turning,
which increases exposure and raises the stakes.
Risks exist at all levels; more time at the lathe
means more exposure and a greater need for the
next step in protection.
Powered Air Purifying Respirators (PAPRs) combine
impact-rated visors with powered airflow and highefficiency filtration. PAPRs and HEPA-rated systems
(≥99.97% down to 0.3 microns) are widely considered the gold standard for respiratory protection in
woodworking. This article documents my personal
path through the options toward a better solution
at the lathe.
2. What PAPRs Add
PAPRs don’t replace dust collection. Good practice
still starts with a latheside collector and ceiling filtration. PAPRs add a personal layer to keep the air
you breathe clean.
Unlike N95 or N100 masks (which pull air through
dense media), PAPRs use a blower to deliver clean
air under positive pressure. That supports natural
breathing, keeps dust outside the enclosure, and
helps prevent fogging.
With visors meeting impact standards, PAPRs
guard against chips and catastrophic failures that
can send fragments outward. Some models further
integrate head coverage, protecting the face, eyes,
lungs, and skull.
There are trade-offs. PAPRs add gear - either an
enclosed headpiece or a headpiece plus a waistmounted filtration unit. Extra equipment takes adjustment and can feel
bulkier than a mask or
shield.
Some
turners
experiment with DIY powered
shields. While inventive,
those rarely meet formal
safety standards. This
article focuses on certified PAPRs intended for
dependable,
long-term
protection.
3. PAPR Models Under Consideration
To anchor the comparison, I included the Uvex
S8500 Bionic Face Shield with an N95 mask as a
baseline that many of us already use.
4. Process of Elimination
Filtration + impact protection (baseline: Uvex +
N95):
The solution needed to match or exceed my current Uvex S8500 + N95 baseline: high-impact visor
and fine dust filtration.
Eliminated: Peke PowerCap Active IP and
Sundström SR 580: only medium-impact visors, below the baseline noted earlier.
Remaining: Trend Airshield Pro, Air3, Sundström SR
570 + SR 500 and 3M M307 + TR302N+. All remain-
(Continued on page 6)

ing systems provide certified HEPA filtration, so filtration was no longer a differentiator.
Head protection:
Not initially a deciding factor for this comparison,
though bump caps and industrial helmets can
strengthen overall frames. Since my Uvex baseline
doesn’t offer either, this added protection wasn’t
immediately relevant to my search, and I chose to
set head protection standards aside at this stage.
Battery type and runtime:
Years ago, I eliminated non-Li-ion tools from my
workshop. My current tools charge quickly, last
long, and have no memory effect. I’m not willing to
revisit NiMH.
Eliminated: Trend Airshield Pro (NiMH battery;
heavier and less efficient).
Remaining: Air3, Sundström SR 570 + SR 500 and
3M M307 + TR302N+.

Notes
•
Uvex, Trend, Air3, and 3M M307 all meet the ANSI Z87.1+ high-impact standard. This designation
means the visor has passed high-velocity impact tests (a steel ball fired at 300 ft/sec).
•
Sundström’s 580 + SR 500 heavy industrial system surprisingly offers only medium impact visors, but
Sundström confirms that their Sundström SR 570 with the standard polycarbonate mask does meet
the ANSI Z87.1+ high-impact standard.
•
Designs vary: headpiece-only vs. waist-mounted blowers, each affecting comfort and workflow.
•
Battery technology: all except Trend use modern lithium-ion packs, offering longer runtimes and
lighter weight than NiMH batteries.

January 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
Comfort and workflow:
Headpiece-only units are simpler but can feel
heavy. Waist-mounted blowers shift weight off the
head but add hoses and belt packs. In practice,
Air3, Sundström SR 570 and 3M M-307 with hose
all weigh about 850 g on the head (excluding waistworn filter), so head weight isn’t decisive.
How this weight is distributed can be a key factor
for comfort. I’ve worn the 3M and found it ok. The
turners I chatted with who have an Air3 report that
the weight is well-distributed and remarkably comfortable. I have no experience with the Sundström
SR 570.
The Trend Airshield Pro, eliminated earlier on my
personal subjective desire not to have NiMH
batteries back in my shop, has been criticized as
front-heavy and poorly balanced.
5. Cost Comparison
Price was the final factor in narrowing the field.
While safety and workflow matter hugely, the reality is that these systems represent very different
levels of investment.
The pricing for our shortlisted products are:
•
Air3: $919 CAD (plus taxes and duties) for the
complete kit, or $778 CAD for the respirator
alone. With a 10% promo code, either Keith
Gotschall’s KEITH10 or MicroClimates 10AIR3,
the respirator price drops to about $700 CAD
before taxes and duties. Consumables are modest: filters $126 CAD per set, visor $98, shroud
$41, headgear $55, and tear-offs $55. Even
with regular filter changes, ongoing costs remain predictable and manageable for an individual turner.
•
Sundström SR 570 + SR 500: $2,316.95 CAD
from Woodchuckers, this package includes the
SR 500 fan unit, SR 570 face shield with bump
cap, breathing hose, battery and charger, belt,
flow meter, two filter covers, filter adapters,
and HE filters. Consumables are notably modest in cost, coming in well below those for the
Air3 and 3M systems, with a two-pack of replacement filters running only $32.75 CAD.
•
3M
Versaflo
Heavy
Industry
PAPR
Kit
TR300HIK: $2,635 CAD currently on Amazon.com (includes shipping and import charges), includes the M307 helmet, blower, filters,
battery, and charger. Replacement filters run
$70–$180 CAD per pack. This makes the 3M
solution almost four times the upfront cost of
Air3.
6. Looking Ahead: Stability vs. Innovation
3M is a global industrial supplier with decades of
proven reliability. Versaflo has shipped thousands
of units worldwide, and 3M’s scale supports long-
(Continued from page 6)
(Continued on page 8)
MicroClimate Air3
Sundstrom SR 500 SR 570

January 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
term availability of filters, batteries, and parts. For
turners who value stability and guaranteed support, 3M is the safe bet.
Sundström, by contrast, operates on a smaller
scale but has built a strong reputation in Europe
and among specialized users. The SR 570 + SR 500
system offers industrial-grade protection at a lower
entry cost than 3M, with consumables priced far
more modestly. For those concerned about lifetime
affordability, Sundström represents a pragmatic
middle ground: proven engineering without 3M’s
global dominance.
Both 3M and Sundström also stand apart in offering solutions that integrate into a full helmet or
bump-cap system. This distinction shouldn’t be underestimated: a helmet or bump-cap frame provides structural protection for the head as well as
the face, and can strengthen the overall safety envelope in ways that a visor-only certified design
cannot. For turners who value that added layer of
resilience, these integrated systems represent a
meaningful advantage.
MicroClimate’s Air3 is from a younger company
with far fewer units shipped. Long-term parts and
support are less certain. Yet the Air3 is making
waves in the woodturning community: well-known
turners, including Kevin Jesequel and Keith
Gotschall, are appearing with it in demonstrations
and online. Their adoption suggests the Air3 is a
serious option for comfort, visibility, and modern
design — at a fraction of the cost of either 3M or
Sundström.
The comparison highlights three viable approaches:
•
3M Versaflo M307 system — industrial grade,
proven, backed by a company that will be here
tomorrow, but at a high cost.
•
Sundström SR 570 + SR 500 system — robust,
well-engineered, with consumables priced well
below 3M, and at a lower entry cost.
•
MicroClimate Air3 — innovative, ergonomic,
gaining credibility through respected turners,
but dependent on a younger company’s future,
at a fraction of the cost of either 3M or
Sundström.
7. Air3 MicroClimate Responds to My Concerns
As part of my research, I contacted MicroClimate
directly with a question about the ANSI Z87.1+ high
-impact rating. I asked whether the rating applied
only to the visor itself or to the visor as mounted
within the Air3 system. From the product images, it
appeared that the visor is held in place by the air
filters, and I wanted to know whether this design
might allow the visor to detach during high-impact
events.
Miguel Lazaro, Chief Engineer at MicroClimate,
provided a detailed response. He confirmed that
the visor meets the same high-impact standard
noted earlier, and that MicroClimate also tests the
visor mounted on the Air3 base and filters. These
tests are conducted both at a third-party facility
and again at their Utah site when batches of parts
are received to confirm each batch meets standards.
According to Lazaro, the visor is secured at the
front and rear by the Air3 base, and on the sides by
the installed filters. In repeated high-impact tests
— he explained as striking the visor with a steel
ball travelling at over 300 feet per second — the
visor has never detached, and the filters have remained properly seated.
MicroClimate also shared a real-world report from
a woodturner whose Air3 was struck by a large
(Continued from page 7)
(Continued on page 9)
3M Versaflo TR-300-HIK Kit

January 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
fragment
ejected
at
high speed. In that case,
the filters were forced
out of the base, but the
visor still provided protection, and the user
was unharmed. While
anecdotal, it adds confidence that the system
provides
meaningful
protection even beyond
its rated test conditions.
8. My decision
After weighing visor protection, filtration, workflow, and cost, I am leaning toward the Air3. As
noted earlier, it comes in at about one-quarter the
cost of the 3M system, while still offering HEPA filtration, high-impact visor protection, and a design
that many turners report as comfortable and wellbalanced.
The complete kit adds little beyond conveniences,
so I plan to purchase only the respirator. A standard charger and my own storage solutions will
suffice.
Air3 is a younger company, and several demonstrators received their units at no cost, so I remain cautious. Still, adoption by respected turners and my
direct correspondence with MicroClimate reassure
me that it is a viable option.
I also recognize that helmet and bump-cap systems
from 3M and Sundström likely provide superior
structural protection — an advantage that deserves real consideration. But they also come
at a significantly higher
cost, and my immediate
goal was to find a solution that clearly improves on my Uvex +
N95 baseline while staying within a more practical budget. For my shop
and workflow, Air3 represents
that
balance
point.
I expect I will order the Air3. My biggest reservation is the lack of a local retailer or anywhere I can
do a hands-on review before purchase. If the visor’s mounting proves less secure than promised, I
will reserve it for sanding and fall back on my baseline: a Uvex face shield paired with an N95 mask.
That fallback remains ready and reliable in my
shop.
9. Closing Reflection
Every turner must make their own decision. The
details and specifications are extensive, and my
interpretation is my own; yours may differ. Weigh
all available information, consider your priorities,
and choose what fits your shop and workflow.
What I’ve offered here is not a prescription, but a
record of moving from uninformed to narrowing
the field and arriving at a choice — or almost a
choice. For me, the balance of cost, comfort, and
community adoption leans toward Air3, though
Uvex + N95 remains a strong baseline that can’t be
ignored. At the same time, I may yet bite the bullet
and invest in a 3M system.
Availability also plays a role — without local retailers, some solutions remain harder to evaluate
hands-on, and that reality shapes the choices we
make.
In the end, this journey is about clarity, not certainty. Each turner will find their own balance of stability, innovation, and practicality. And if fogged glasses aren’t worth $700 to solve, I may treat myself to
a couple of gouges instead.
Disclaimer: This article reflects my personal research and experiences as a woodturner. It is not
intended as professional safety advice or a formal
endorsement of any specific product. Standards
and specifications are noted to the best of my understanding, but readers should consult manufacturer documentation and occupational health guidance before making decisions about protective
equipment. Each turner’s shop, workflow, and priorities differ, and the responsibility for final choices
rests with the individual.

Kiss the Baby -Thoughts on Critique
By Robert (Bob) Gilson (Editing and encouragement
- Art Liestman)
A woman and her baby get on a bus and as she
pays her fare the bus driver looks at her baby and
comments, “that is the ugliest baby I have ever
seen.” The woman is shocked. She walks to the
back of the bus and sits down beside an elderly
gentleman. She proceeds to tell him what the bus
driver said to her. The man listens and then says, “
I think you need to go right back up to the driver
and give him a piece of your mind and while you’re
doing that I’ll hold your monkey for you."
In everyday speech, criticism is generally seen as an
expression of disapproval of someone or something based on perceived faults or mistakes.
Critique is a more formal analysis of a work intended to provide an informed evaluation. Meanwhile,
constructive criticism is a type of helpful feedback
that aims to help someone improve by highlighting
their strong points and suggesting areas for improvement, accompanied by specific suggestions.
I used to think that everything I made was perfect
and that whenever I displayed something of mine I
thought everyone would want to “to kiss the baby.” If they didn't I'd be bummed out. I thought
“these people can’t judge my work, they never
make anything themselves, they have no experience being creative and besides they only judge
others and never themselves.
When I was growing up I always wanted my family
and friends to appreciate me and the things I
made. I wanted validation and to be accepted. I
became aware of criticism and the fear of criticism
was to be avoided at all costs. A large part of that I
know had to do with my own insecurity, my lack of
self confidence as well as not having any idea of
where I was going or how I was going to get there. I
thought it better to be accepted into the circle than
to be shunned out of it.
As I grew up and started to travel the world I realized that in judging others I was often wrong, my
preconceived notions were often way off base, I
figured my paradigm needed a big shift! I realized
that if I didn’t want to be judged maybe I should be
less judgmental. I started to work on ditching the
notion that others would appreciate everything I
created regardless of how good it was, how creative I was or how well it was presented. Full disclosure, while its gotten easier for me over time, I’m
still working on it. It’s a tough one.
When I was younger my understanding of the creative process was limited. I concluded that if I wanted to develop it I had to see the world through a
wider lens.
What's most important is that we treat ourselves
with loving care and compassion and understand
there is no imperative for others to validate the
things that we do. If you feel good about what you
are creating then that's all that really matters period.
Notwithstanding the above there's much to be
gained from criticism. Constructive criticism is important in fostering your ability to grow as an
artist. If you can see your work through other people eyes you can build the self-confidence necessary to not feel threatened, attacked or belittled.
To treat it simply as information, data input or
feedback that’s essential to your progression as an
artist.
Easier said than done? Putting yourself out there
and having others take shots at you is not a pleasant experience. Here’s the gist of it though, if you
believe in what you're creating has value, if you
believe in yourself, feel confident and like what
you've created then you have made a good start.
When you put a piece of your work on the table
and invite other people to view it and provide you
with feedback you are taking a huge risk and a vital
one.
People could say that’s the ugliest baby they've
ever seen, how could you create something like
that. They could also say OMG that’s beautiful,
(Continued on page 11)

January 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
What if you added a blue wash to accent the lines
in the base or if you altered the curve slightly you
would end up with a pleasing line or if you were to
slightly change the radius of this sphere it would
provide more impact, or if you moved the centre of
the sphere up you would create more emotion.
These are all valid positive comments, constructive
criticism, part of the process of critique. They are
not threatening or hostile in any way and they start
from a neutral place and aim to elevate your work.
They are not saying their way is better, they are
asking you to consider other possibilities.
Critique improves critical and analytical thinking
and hones your evaluative skills.
The principles of critique are describing, analyzing,
interpreting and evaluating.
Accurately describing what you see is a skill that
takes time and attention to detail to develop. Analysis requires broad field knowledge and the ability
to use objective comparisons. Interpreting requires
the synthesis of information and suggestions of
possibilities. Evaluating requires comparisons to
benchmarks set by masters in the field. Critique is
not to be taken lightly and cannot be fobbed off as
mere criticism.
What is a good critique for a woodturner? Being
constructive means coming to the critique with the
ultimate goal of helping the turner improve. It
means criticizing with good intentions. It doesn't
mean coddling or being so nice that you never hear
a hard thing. Nor is it browbeating or being so hard
you’ll never say a nice thing.
The monthly Presidents’ choice challenge not only
offers GVWG members the opportunity to test
your turning skills and to display your work alongside other guild members, It also provides opportunity for critique if you are open to it.
Once the pieces are on the table its hard not to
have a long look at each piece and wonder about
process, finish and form. Its rather stimulating to
talk about your work with others in a constructive
way and I can’t think of a better more supportive
group to do it with than GVWG members.
So bring your baby along to the next Guild meeting.
No one will tell you its ugly, they will appreciate
you for simply getting on the bus.
(Continued from page 10)
KMS Tools Group Rewards
Shopping at KMS Tools means you can help your
club earn credit - approximately 2% on your purchase. For instance, we recently used some of our
credit to buy the brand-new Laguna demo lathe
that we use for Focus on Fundamentals! All you
need to do is to link your name/phone number to
the GVWG and you’re done. The easiest way to do
this is to go online to: https://www.kmstools.com/
group-rewards and fill in a short form. In doing so,
you also become a KMS Club member and benefit
from better pricing on their full line of products. As
a friendly reminder if you are already a KMS Club
member, it is worthwhile to check that you are also
linked to the GVWG for us to receive the credits.

KMS Class Lathe Repair
By Brian Lunt
Thanks to Steve Daschel, we now have a repaired
motor for our KMS Classroom Nova Lathe
For some time now this lathe has been getting
noisier, so it was time to repair and replace the
motor bearings.
Steve ( Dax ) pulled out several “retired” aircraft
repair tools and showed me how to replace bearings.
It was a detailed process making several witness
marks as we took it all apart, so we had guiding
points to reference when re assembling.
Now all we have to do is remount the motor on the
lathe and we can call this job done.
Thanks Dax

January 2026

Cell Phone Holder Drill Press Hack
By Ed Pretty
I bought a cell phone holder to use as a flexible
mount for the duct pickup at my drill press. My
pickup is 2 1/2" ducting, so quite light and I have
shelving nearby to mount the flexible holder on. If
someone wanted to use this setup and didn't have
shelving nearby, it would be an easy thing to make
a wooden clamp that clamps to the column to anchor the holder. The price was right at about $25
on Amazon. Just search for "flexible phone mount".

January 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 14
Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
Like many folks my age, my first experience with
woodturning came in shop class back in the mid-
'70s—grade 8, if memory serves me right. Our
teacher, Mr. Mills (that really was his name), got
me started on the lathe. Looking back now, it’s
clear he didn’t know much about turning. I suspect
he probably picked up the basics during a professional development day, then turned around and
introduced it to a handful of us during shop class.
I was setup at the lathe with a blank already
mounted. The wood was mahogany and was
attached to a faceplate with a sacrificial block and a
brown paper glue line. Somehow, the school had a
huge supply of mahogany planks, two inches thick
and eight to twelve inches wide. To shape the
bowl, I was given a round-nose scraper. It was dull,
though I didn’t realize it at the time, but I do remember that progress was slow and a bit frustrating. When the top was finished, it was separated from the sacrificial block at the glue line using a
planning iron and a mallet. The bottom of the piece
was not turned, only sanded smooth.
My bowl/dish was 11 inches wide, had a shallow
inside arc and straight, thick outside walls. It was
not thing of beauty, but my parents kept it and
stored fruit on it. When I got my own home, it
came with me and I still have it. I also used it as a
fruit bowl. Over time, it has developed stains from
fruit left to spoil, but that has only increased its
character. It space on the counter has now been
retired, replaced by the first natural edge bowl that
I created when I started turning again.
Tell us about your workshop/studio?
I’ve always loved power tools and working with
wood. My dad had a small workshop with a table
saw, chop saw, drill press, and a collection of hand
tools. It wasn’t a studio — more a place to fix
things, tackle home repairs, or cut parts for the HO
model train layout we built together.
When I bought my first home, a workshop was non
-negotiable, though at that stage it was all about
home improvement. Later, when we built our current house, having a dedicated workshop was a top
priority. The space isn’t perfect — a little chopped
up — but it’s mine, and over time it’s grown into
something much more than a workshop.
At first, I tackled larger flat woodworking projects:
a raised-panel curved fireplace mantel, coffee tables, and furniture cabinets. They were rewarding,
but everything was big and slow to finish. I wanted
woodworking to feel fun again. In December 1999,
I bought my first lathe — a Nova Galaxy — just as
my son was home for Christmas to help move it
into the basement shop. That lathe opened the
door to woodturning, and soon I was collecting
gouges, scrapers, and sharpening tools.
(Continued on page 15)

By Don Gamble with Diana Dougherty

During COVID, the shop became a refuge, a place
to learn and experiment. By March 2022, I was
ready to take things further and ordered a Oneway
2436 lathe. After a six-month wait, it finally arrived
in September. With the help of my son and a
neighbour, we maneuvered it around the outside
of the house, down a hill, and into the shop —
ready to go by October.
Since then, the studio has steadily evolved. I’ve
added a slow-speed grinder with CBN wheels, a
Tormek T-8, a Magnum 14” bandsaw, several
chainsaws, a home-built cyclone dust extractor,
ceiling-mounted filtration, and most recently, carving and pyrography tools.
Today, my workshop is more than a place to build
— it’s where I explore, learn, and create. It’s not
perfect, but it’s dedicated, well-equipped, and always evolving, just like my journey in woodturning.
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
My go-to tool is a Thompson 5/8” V bowl gouge,
which I purchased shortly after buying the Oneway
lathe. At first, it was a painful relationship — the Vshaped flute was tricky to sharpen without creating
a dip behind the nose. Over time, I learned to overcome that challenge, and now I sharpen both the
5/8” and ½” Thompson gouges to a 55° angle following Glenn Lucas’s recommendations. The 5/8”
gouge, with its long handle braced against my
thigh, is my workhorse for shearing pull cuts that
refine the outside form of bowls and hollow forms.
Many of my tool choices have been influenced by
classes. In a session with Ed Pretty, we used Woodworkers Specialties gouges sharpened at 45°. I was
impressed by how the 45° bevel and polished flute
produced such a sharp cutting edge. After that
class, I purchased both the 5/8” and ½” doubleended gouges from Woodworkers Specialties. I
keep them sharpened at 45° and use them extensively on second-turned bowls to achieve crisp,
clean cuts on the lip and top inside. The doubleended design is a bonus — a quick flip gives me a
fresh edge without leaving the lathe.
Another turning point came in a class with Tom
Wirsing, where we learned to sharpen and use negative rake scrapers (NRS). Since then, I’ve added
several to my arsenal. My 1” x ¼” Thompson scraper has been reground to a NRS with a 22.5° angle
on both sides, and I also use a Glenn Lucas French
Curve scraper, 3/8” thick, sharpened to 33° on
each side. The 1” NRS is ideal for cleaning up tearout and making micro-adjustments to exterior
curves, while the French Curve scraper excels inside bowls, removing bumps and tool marks with
precision.
What is your favourite wood?
I don’t know if I truly have a single favourite wood.
I’ve turned a lot of maple simply because it’s
what’s most available. Cherry, on the other hand,
turns beautifully — but I’ve collected and processed more cherry than I could use quickly, and
too often it ended up as firewood.
One of my most memorable experiences was
spending a week at Glenn Lucas’s studio in Ireland.
We turned a variety of Irish woods, and every one
of them was excellent. I suspect that had less to do
with the species and more to do with Glenn’s careful cutting and drying processes.
In general, I twice-turn everything, so green wood
is my favourite. It’s forgiving, lively, and full of potential. Old, forgotten dry wood is my least favour-

ite — it tends to fight back. But whatever the species or condition, each piece carries a story trapped
inside it, waiting to be revealed on the lathe.
What finishes do you prefer using?
When I first started turning, the fun was in how
quickly I could create something. For that reason, I
began with a friction polish — a mix of denatured
alcohol, shellac, and boiled linseed oil in roughly
equal parts. It was fast, easy, and gave a nice shine,
so I used it for several years.
As people began asking if they could actually use
my bowls, I realized that finish wouldn’t hold up
well. That sent me looking for alternatives. I experimented briefly with walnut oil, which produced a
pleasant surface but took far too long to dry for my
liking.
Today, I prefer Osmo TopOil. I apply two coats, and
it gives a durable, food-safe finish that isn’t glossy.
When I do want a shiny piece, I’ll use the Beall
buffing system, which produces a high-polish surface.
Lately, my focus has shifted toward texture and
color. Some of my recent pieces have been finished
entirely with acrylic paints, opening up new creative directions beyond traditional clear finishes.
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
No
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
Family is my first and most important interest, and
much of what I do — whether in the shop or outdoors - connects back to spending time with them.
I also enjoy fly fishing on both lakes and rivers.
I’ve always been drawn to creating, which led me
to study Computer Science and spend years programming, including building CAD tools early in my
career. During COVID, I built a CNC using 3Dprinted parts and now support a GitHub project
that provides the Fusion 360 post-processor to
drive it. Alongside this, I share ongoing 3D-printed
designs on Thingiverse, including cases and addons for the CNC.
For woodturning, I run a YouTube channel called
DG Workshop and a Facebook page to share projects and connect with the turning community. I’ve
also become active with the Greater Vancouver
Woodturners Guild (GVWG), helping launch the
new guild website.
Most recently, I’ve begun exploring AI as a mentor
in texturing and coloring. I knew nothing about coloring or painting when I started, but by working
with AI as a guide I’ve been able to educate myself
and continue expanding into this creative area.
What inspires you – where do you get your
ideas from?
There are just so many ideas and forms out there
to try. Often it will be from a turner on Instagram
or what a guest demonstrator did in a demonstration or class.

Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
That’s hard to say. I find that I take something
away from every demo, class or video I watch.
Spending a week with Glenn Lucas was an incredible experience in learning, but also in spending
dedicated time with other turners.
Where do you usually display and/or sell your
work?
I’ve only displayed my work at guild meetings and
have not yet sold my work. Most pieces have been
given to friends or as wedding or engagement gifts.
What is the most challenging piece that you
have made so far?
Everything when it is the first time is the most challenging. I don’t think I’ve turned many or anything.
I remember preparing to go to visit Glenn Lucus in
Ireland and thinking, “I’ve never turned a platter!”
So, I went out and turned three identical platters
before leaving. The first was very challenging, but
by the third it was much simpler.
Currently, I’m exploring texture and color. When I
started, I had a limited feel for texture, but with
painting and color I felt totally disarmed. This is
likely the biggest learning opportunity for me, but I
wouldn’t describe the pieces I’ve made as a challenge.
What is your favorite project to date?
I think the textured and colored pieces that I’ve
most recently done. They allowed me to learn and
explore my visions. I think they are the closest
things that I’ve created that I would call art.
Where do you see your work going in the future?
I hope to learn a lot more and share the learning
with others. I hope that my techniques refine and
that someday someone will say, I like that artwork.
Are there any new techniques you would like
to try?
Yes, but I don’t know what they are today. Likely
something I see at a demo tomorrow or next week,
or a conversation I have with someone, or a vision I
share with an AI as I explore what is possible.

Safety Guidelines for Woodturning
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 40)

January 2026
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 40
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
